item_name: City of London Police and other forces operating LFR in Greater London
operator: Composite item covering (a) City of London Police, the territorial force for the Square Mile, and (b) the five territorial forces bordering Greater London - Essex Police, Surrey Police (operating jointly with Sussex Police), Kent Police, Hertfordshire Constabulary, and Thames Valley Police (operating jointly with Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary). Also covers joint and national programmes: the Home Office LFR van fund and the NPCC/College of Policing framework under which all of them operate.
vendor: No single vendor, because there is no single system. Essex Police uses Corsight AI - the only UK force to have picked a non-NEC LFR supplier, and the reason its algorithm has been separately tested by the National Physical Laboratory and Cambridge University. The Metropolitan Police and British Transport Police both use NEC NeoFace. The vendor behind the Home Office-funded van fleet issued to Surrey/Sussex, Thames Valley/Hampshire, Bedfordshire, Greater Manchester and West Yorkshire is not consistently identified in public sources and is most likely NEC NeoFace under the national framework. City of London Police has no LFR vendor because it has no LFR system. [uncertain]
london_coverage_summary: The headline finding is a negative one, and it is well evidenced: neither City of London Police nor any neighbouring force operates live facial recognition inside the Greater London boundary. City of London Police is absent from every published list of forces using LFR, including Statewatch's June 2026 enumeration of the twelve forces known to have used it and Big Brother Watch's tracking of the Home Office van rollout; its own police authority's outstanding-references log shows members merely asking officers in June 2025 to 'look into the issue of facial recognition', with no response recorded and no programme since. The five bordering forces do run LFR, but exclusively in their own towns - Chelmsford, Southend and Colchester (Essex); Redhill (Surrey/Sussex); Chatham (Kent); Watford and Stevenage (Hertfordshire); Slough, Aylesbury, Bicester and Oxford (Thames Valley) - and no deployment by any of them inside Greater London has been documented. Within the Greater London boundary, live facial recognition is run by exactly two forces: the Metropolitan Police and British Transport Police, both covered as separate items in this survey. The Square Mile is, as of September 2026, the one part of central London with no police LFR at all.
camera_count_claimed: Zero is also the claimed figure - no operator in this item claims any LFR camera inside Greater London. Adjacent published figures, for scale and for the avoidance of double-counting: the Home Office is funding an increase from 10 to 50 LFR vans nationally over five years (announced January 2026); Surrey and Sussex received two vans jointly; twelve forces in England and Wales are known to have used LFR by June 2026, and City of London Police is not among them. The only historical claim attaching to City of London Police is a 2019 proposal, reported at the time, for 'widescale integration' of public and private CCTV networks into a facial-recognition 'ring of steel' around the City - a plan that appears never to have been implemented and for which no 2025 or 2026 corroboration was found. [uncertain]
fixed_vs_mobile: Zero fixed and zero mobile inside Greater London, for every operator in this item. Outside the boundary the pattern is uniformly mobile: all five neighbouring forces use marked van-mounted LFR units, mostly Home Office-funded, parked in a town centre for a single shift and signposted. None of them has installed a permanent LFR camera anywhere. Fixed LFR in the London region is a Metropolitan Police phenomenon only - the Croydon pilot of static cameras at each end of the High Street (October 2025 to March 2026) and the announced installation of static cameras on lampposts across the West End and Soho by the end of 2026, with further areas trailed for 2027. Neither the Croydon nor the West End scheme extends into the City of London, which is a separate police area the Met does not cover, and no source reviewed places any static LFR camera inside the Square Mile.
geographic_concentration: The concentration is entirely OUTSIDE Greater London, in each force's own town centres, and this matters for a London map because these sites should not be plotted as London cameras. Nearest documented sites by force: ESSEX - Chelmsford, Southend-on-Sea, Colchester, plus Clacton Airshow (22 August 2026); Essex's Metropolitan-facing boundary towns such as Romford and Ilford are policed by the Met, not Essex Police, so Essex LFR does not reach the London fringe. SURREY and SUSSEX - two shared Home Office vans, first deployed at Redhill in November 2025; no deployment documented at Kingston, Sutton or the Croydon boundary, and Croydon LFR is Met-operated. KENT - Chatham town centre over two days; the Kent PCC has publicly said public consent would be needed for any wider use. HERTFORDSHIRE - trial launched December 2025, Watford High Street on 27 February 2026 (four arrests), Stevenage town centre on 1 May 2026; Watford is the closest documented non-Met LFR site to Greater London, roughly three miles beyond the boundary at Harrow. THAMES VALLEY and HAMPSHIRE - repeated deployments at Slough High Street (February, April, May and 23 July 2026), Aylesbury town centre (first in April 2026, and again later in 2026), plus Bicester and Oxford; Slough is the closest Thames Valley site to London, about four miles west of Hillingdon. Inside Greater London the clusters belong to other items: the Met in Croydon, the West End, Soho, Stratford and at Notting Hill Carnival, and BTP at the mainline termini and Underground stations.
last_confirmed_active_date: Not applicable for City of London Police - there is no date on which it has ever been confirmed to operate LFR, and the most recent relevant record is its police authority's June 2025 outstanding-reference asking officers to look into facial recognition, still logged without a response. For the neighbouring forces, the most recent confirmed activity outside the boundary is 25-26 August 2026 (Essex Police, Southend, two arrests) and 22 August 2026 (Essex Police, Clacton Airshow, three arrests), with Thames Valley's Slough deployment on 23 July 2026 and Hertfordshire's Stevenage deployment on 1 May 2026 also well documented. The last confirmed date on which any of these operators ran LFR INSIDE Greater London is: none, ever.
evidence_of_current_activity: The evidence here cuts two ways and both directions should be stated plainly. Evidence that the neighbouring forces are actively running LFR in 2026: Essex Police resumed deployments after its pause and reported 22 deployments producing 57 arrests from 353,000 faces scanned with no false positive matches (reported July 2026), then further arrests at Clacton on 22 August and Southend on 25-26 August 2026; Thames Valley published per-deployment results for Slough on 23 July 2026 (14,795 faces, four alerts, three outcomes, watchlist of 3,389); Hertfordshire published its Watford result on 27 February 2026 and pre-announced Stevenage for 1 May 2026. Each of these forces maintains a public LFR page listing upcoming and completed deployments. Evidence that none of this touches Greater London: every one of those published deployment locations is outside the boundary, and no source reviewed records a cross-border LFR operation. Evidence that City of London Police has nothing running: its absence from Statewatch's June 2026 list of twelve LFR-using forces, from Big Brother Watch's list of the three original plus seven new adopters, and from all reported Home Office van allocations; plus the unanswered June 2025 committee reference. Absence of evidence is weaker than a denial, but four independent enumerations all omitting the same force is strong.
known_pauses_or_withdrawals: The most significant is Essex Police, the only force in this group to have suspended LFR outright. Deployments were paused for an Information Commissioner's Office audit, and reporting in March 2026 described a halt over accuracy and bias risks after the force had scanned around 2.5 million faces on algorithm settings later judged wrong. The ICO audit ultimately gave 'reasonable data protection assurance' while warning that all forces must routinely test for bias. Two independent evaluations of the Corsight system landed in March 2026 and disagreed: the National Physical Laboratory measured an 89% true positive identification rate against a 0.017% false positive rate (about 1 in 5,700) on an 18,000-image watchlist and found no statistically significant gender or ethnicity bias, while a Cambridge University evaluation found the system statistically more likely to correctly identify Black people and men, raising separate fairness questions. Essex resumed deployments after the evaluations. Note that sources date the pause inconsistently - some describe a pause from August 2025 with redeployment in April, others a halt reported in March 2026 - and there may have been two distinct suspensions rather than one; the exact chronology could not be resolved. [uncertain] Kent Police's PCC has publicly conditioned any wider Kent use on public consent, which is a brake rather than a withdrawal. No force in this group has abandoned LFR, and City of London Police has never started, so it has nothing to withdraw.
publication_channel: Split by operator. City of London Police: nothing to publish, and no LFR transparency page exists on its site. The neighbouring forces all publish, to a reasonable standard: Essex Police at https://www.essex.police.uk/police-forces/essex-police/areas/essex-police/au/about-us/live-facial-recognition/ with a supporting policy document D 2700 at https://www.essex.police.uk/foi-ai/essex-police/our-policies-and-procedures/d/d-2700-policy-live-facial-recognition/ ; Surrey Police at https://www.surrey.police.uk/police-forces/surrey-police/areas/au/about-us/live-facial-recognition/ and Sussex Police at https://www.sussex.police.uk/police-forces/sussex-police/areas/au/about-us/governance-and-processes/live-facial-recognition/ , both committing to publicise deployment locations in advance and to signpost the vans; Hertfordshire Constabulary at https://www.herts.police.uk/police-forces/hertfordshire-constabulary/areas/about-us/live-facial-recognition-lfr-technology/live-facial-recognition-lfr-technology/ ; Thames Valley Police at https://www.thamesvalley.police.uk/police-forces/thames-valley-police/areas/au/about-us/live-facial-recognition-technology/ with a separate results register at https://www.thamesvalley.police.uk/police-forces/thames-valley-police/areas/sd/stats-and-data/live-facial-recognition-deployments-and-results/ , which is the best of the group - it gives per-deployment faces scanned, alerts, outcomes and watchlist size. Note that most UK police domains sit behind a Cloudflare interstitial that blocks automated retrieval, so these pages are cited from their published URLs and from reporting of their contents rather than direct fetch.
live_feed_or_map_available: No, and this is the clearest answer in the whole file. There is no live feed, no map and no machine-readable endpoint for any operator in this item - not official, not third-party. For City of London Police the question does not arise: there are no cameras to show. For the five neighbouring forces the transparency that exists is a text list of upcoming town-centre deployments on each force's own website, published force by force, in five different places, in five different formats, with no coordinates, no common schema, no feed and no aggregation. Nobody publishes a single map of UK police LFR deployments, and no third party maintains one covering these forces. Thames Valley's deployments-and-results register is the nearest thing to structured data anywhere in this group, and it is a retrospective HTML table of town names, not a live location service. For a London mapping project the practical consequence is simple: there is nothing here to plot and nothing to poll, and the correct representation of City of London Police and the neighbouring forces on a map of London facial recognition cameras is an explicit absence, not an empty gap that implies missing data.
advance_notice_period: No force in this group publishes a guaranteed minimum. Surrey, Sussex, Essex, Hertfordshire and Thames Valley all commit to publicising the location before the van is deployed and to signposting it on the day; observed practice ranges from several days ahead (Hertfordshire pre-announced the 1 May 2026 Stevenage deployment well in advance, and Essex published a forward schedule of deployments through early August 2026) down to a day or less. Not applicable to City of London Police. [uncertain]
foi_or_audit_sources: The strongest audit material in this item concerns Essex: the ICO's audit of Essex Police's LFR, which concluded 'reasonable data protection assurance' with a warning about routine bias testing, alongside the ICO's March 2026 statement on data protection and responsible police facial recognition; the National Physical Laboratory's evaluation of the Corsight algorithm; and the Cambridge University evaluation that reached a different conclusion on demographic differentials. Statewatch's June 2026 analysis is the most useful single enumeration of which forces use which variant of facial recognition, and is the primary basis for the finding that City of London Police uses none. Big Brother Watch tracks the national rollout and named the seven new adopter forces. The POST (Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology) briefing on facial recognition technology in policing and Liberty's facial recognition material give the national legal picture. The City of London Police Authority Board and Local Policing Committee papers on democracy.cityoflondon.gov.uk are the primary source for the force's own position, specifically the outstanding-references log recording the unanswered June 2025 request that officers look into facial recognition. No FOI response was located that directly asks City of London Police whether it operates LFR - such an FOI would be the single most valuable next step to convert this file's well-supported negative inference into a documented denial.
legal_basis: Identical in kind for every force here: common law policing powers plus the statutory duty to prevent and detect crime, with biometric processing under Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018 (law enforcement processing), supported per force by a Data Protection Impact Assessment, an Equality Impact Assessment and an Appropriate Policy Document, and operating within the College of Policing and NPCC authorised professional practice for LFR. Essex Police's D 2700 policy is a published worked example. There is still no dedicated UK statute for facial recognition: the Home Office opened a public consultation on a legal framework at the end of 2025 and the King's Speech in May 2026 announced plans for one, but no legislation had been laid before Parliament, and the biometrics commissioners warned in May 2026 that a statutory framework could still be around three years away. City of London Police has no LFR legal basis to state because it runs no LFR; its extensive Square Mile camera and ANPR estate - the 'ring of steel' - is number-plate and conventional CCTV surveillance, which is a different technology and a different legal question, and should not be conflated with facial recognition on a map of facial recognition cameras.
regulatory_challenges: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058 remains the foundational authority, finding that force's deployment unlawful on discretion, DPIA and public sector equality duty grounds rather than condemning LFR in principle. The decisive recent case is R (Thompson and Carlo) v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis, judgment 21 April 2026, in which the High Court dismissed a challenge to the Met's 2024 LFR policy and held it had sufficient clarity, foreseeability and safeguards to satisfy the ECHR quality-of-law standard under Articles 8, 10 and 11; Shaun Thompson had been wrongly stopped after being matched to his brother, and Big Brother Watch signalled an intention to appeal. That judgment concerns Met policy but is the permissive backdrop against which every force in this item now operates. Big Brother Watch has separately launched legal challenges arising from police and retailer misidentifications. The live regulatory pressure on this group specifically is the ICO's Essex audit and its insistence on routine bias testing, and the unresolved conflict between the NPL and Cambridge evaluations of Corsight. No court case or ICO enforcement action against City of London Police over facial recognition exists, because it has no facial recognition to challenge.
oversight_body: For City of London Police, the City of London Police Authority Board and its Local Policing Committee (part of the City of London Corporation), which is where any future LFR decision would surface first and is therefore the place to watch. For each neighbouring force, its own Police and Crime Commissioner - the Kent PCC's public position that any Kent use needs public consent is an example of that oversight actually biting, as is the Herts PCC's announcement of the Hertfordshire trial. Across all of them: the Information Commissioner's Office for data protection; the Biometrics and Surveillance Camera Commissioner function, now largely absorbed into the Investigatory Powers Commissioner's Office and Home Office; the College of Policing and NPCC for operational standards; HMICFRS for force inspection; and the courts by judicial review. No body has cross-force jurisdiction specifically over facial recognition, which is the structural gap that both the Home Office consultation and the promised legislation are meant to close. The Mayor of London and MOPAC have no jurisdiction over any force in this item - including City of London Police, which sits outside the Met's governance entirely.
key_uncertainties: 1) THE CENTRAL FINDING IS A NEGATIVE, AND NEGATIVES ARE HARDER TO PROVE. That City of London Police operates no LFR rests on consistent absence from four independent enumerations (Statewatch June 2026, Big Brother Watch's adopter list, reported Home Office van allocations, and press coverage of the twelve using forces) plus its own police authority's unanswered June 2025 request that officers look into the issue. No source contains an explicit statement by the force that it does not use LFR. A targeted FOI to City of London Police is the cheapest way to convert this from strong inference to documented fact, and should be treated as the outstanding action on this item. 2) THE CAMERAS LIST IS DELIBERATELY EMPTY, AND THAT IS THE ANSWER, NOT A GAP. No operator in this item has a facial recognition camera inside Greater London, so there is nothing to plot. The five neighbouring forces' real deployment sites - Chelmsford, Southend, Colchester, Redhill, Chatham, Watford, Stevenage, Slough, Aylesbury, Bicester, Oxford - are all outside the boundary and were deliberately not entered as cameras, because putting them on a map of London would misrepresent both the forces and the map. They are recorded in geographic_concentration instead. 3) NO CROSS-BORDER OPERATION WAS FOUND, BUT NONE WAS RULED OUT EITHER. Mutual aid into London for major events is routine policing practice, and an LFR van lent to the Met for, say, a state occasion or a large protest would be a plausible unrecorded edge case. Nothing found supports it - Notting Hill Carnival 2026 LFR was Met-operated - but a negative here is weaker than for City of London Police because no enumeration of mutual-aid LFR exists at all. 4) ESSEX'S PAUSE CHRONOLOGY IS GENUINELY CONFUSED IN THE SOURCES, with some describing a pause from August 2025 with redeployment in April and others a halt reported in March 2026; there may have been two separate suspensions. The bias evidence is also unresolved on its merits, with NPL and Cambridge reaching different conclusions about the same algorithm. 5) VENDOR FOR THE HOME OFFICE VAN FLEET is not consistently published; Essex's Corsight is confirmed, the Met's and BTP's NEC NeoFace is confirmed, but the supplier for the Surrey/Sussex and Thames Valley/Hampshire vans is inferred rather than sourced. 6) RETROSPECTIVE FACIAL RECOGNITION IS A MUCH BIGGER BLANK THAN LIVE. This file, like the survey, is about live cameras, but City of London Police almost certainly conducts retrospective facial recognition searches against the Police National Database like other forces, and Thames Valley's retrospective system was referenced in reporting of a misidentification case. RFR needs no camera of its own - it runs on footage already recorded - so a force with zero LFR cameras can still be doing substantial facial recognition. Nothing about the volume, database or governance of RFR use by City of London Police could be established, and it is the single largest unmeasured surveillance surface in this item. 7) MOST UK POLICE WEBSITES ARE CLOUDFLARE-PROTECTED against automated retrieval, so force LFR pages could not be read directly and their contents are cited from published URLs plus reporting; a human opening those pages in a browser would get more current deployment schedules than could be captured here. 8) FORWARD RISK: the Met's static LFR expansion reaches the West End and Soho by end of 2026 with further areas trailed for 2027, and the promised facial recognition legislation is pending. If either the Met's footprint or a national framework pushes LFR into the Square Mile, City of London Police's position could change quickly, and this item should be re-checked rather than trusted as stable.

sources.title: England: Police use of facial recognition technology growing rapidly (Statewatch)
sources.what_it_supports: The single most important source for this file. Enumerates the twelve forces known to have used live facial recognition in England and Wales - Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Essex, Greater Manchester, Metropolitan, Norfolk, North Wales, South Wales, Suffolk, Surrey and Sussex, Thames Valley and Hampshire, West Yorkshire - and CITY OF LONDON POLICE IS NOT AMONG THEM. Also distinguishes live, retrospective and operator-initiated facial recognition, and gives Essex's 2024-25 figures (2.2m faces scanned, 117 arrests).

sources.title: City of London Police - Local Policing Committee outstanding references, June 2025 (PDF)
sources.what_it_supports: PRIMARY SOURCE on City of London Police's own position. The outstanding-references log records, against June 2025 item 5: 'Members asked that Officers look into the issue of facial recognition', assigned to the Commissioner, with the response column left blank. Evidence that facial recognition was an open question rather than an operational programme, and that the City of London Police Authority is the body where any change would first appear.

sources.title: Unprecedented Expansion of Facial Recognition Is 'Worrying for Democracy' (Big Brother Watch)
sources.what_it_supports: Names the seven forces buying LFR to join the original three (Met, South Wales, Essex): Greater Manchester, West Yorkshire, Surrey, Sussex, Bedfordshire, Thames Valley, and Hampshire and Isle of Wight. Independent corroboration that City of London Police is not an adopter.

sources.title: Live facial recognition vans spread across seven additional UK cities (Biometric Update)
sources.what_it_supports: The Home Office van rollout to Greater Manchester, West Yorkshire, Bedfordshire, Surrey, Sussex, Thames Valley and Hampshire, joining the Met, South Wales and Essex. Establishes the van-mounted (mobile, not fixed) form factor for every neighbouring force.

sources.title: Cops get more facial recognition vans as UK bets big on AI policing (The Register)
sources.what_it_supports: The January 2026 Home Office commitment to raise the national LFR van fleet from 10 to 50, and the absence of a published per-force allocation - the basis for treating future spread to any given force as unknown.

sources.title: Live Facial Recognition rolled out in Surrey (Surrey Police)
sources.what_it_supports: Surrey and Sussex received two Home Office LFR vans jointly; first deployment at Redhill in November 2025; commitment to publicise deployment locations in advance and signpost the vans. No Greater London deployment.

sources.title: Live Facial Recognition (LFR) deployment in Watford results in four arrests (Hertfordshire Constabulary)
sources.what_it_supports: Hertfordshire's Watford High Street deployment on 27 February 2026 with four arrests, and pre-announcement of Stevenage town centre for 1 May 2026. Watford is the closest documented non-Met LFR site to the Greater London boundary - and it is still outside it.

sources.title: Live Facial Recognition deployments and results (Thames Valley Police)
sources.what_it_supports: Thames Valley's per-deployment register: Slough High Street on 23 July 2026 (14,795 faces, four alerts, three outcomes, 3,389-record watchlist), the fourth Slough deployment of 2026 after February, April and May, plus Aylesbury, Bicester and Oxford. The best structured transparency of any force in this group - and every location is outside Greater London.

sources.title: Live facial recognition (Essex Police) and policy D 2700
sources.what_it_supports: Essex Police's published deployment schedule and LFR policy. Deployment locations through early August 2026 in Chelmsford, Southend and Colchester; none inside Greater London.

sources.title: Essex Police resume Corsight AI LFR with 57 arrests, no false matches (Biometric Update)
sources.what_it_supports: Essex's resumption after the pause: 22 deployments, 353,000 faces screened, 173 positive alerts, 143 positive interventions, 57 arrests, no false positive matches. Confirms Corsight AI as the vendor and that Essex is active again in 2026.

sources.title: Essex Police halts live facial recognition over bias and accuracy risks (Computer Weekly)
sources.what_it_supports: The Essex suspension over accuracy and bias risk - the only outright pause by any force in this item - and the context of roughly 2.5 million faces having been scanned on settings later judged wrong.

sources.title: Why data protection lies at the heart of responsible police use of facial recognition technology (ICO)
sources.what_it_supports: The regulator's position following its Essex Police audit: 'reasonable data protection assurance' for that force, coupled with the warning that all forces should conduct routine bias testing or risk unfairness.

sources.title: Evaluations of Corsight live facial recognition follow Essex Police pause (Biometric Update)
sources.what_it_supports: The two conflicting independent evaluations: NPL's 89% TPIR at 0.017% FPIR on an 18,000-image watchlist with no statistically significant gender or ethnicity bias, against Cambridge University's finding of demographic differentials.

sources.title: Police and Crime Commissioner says public consent needed for any use of live facial recognition technology in Kent (KentOnline)
sources.what_it_supports: Kent's position: LFR used over two days in Chatham town centre, with the PCC conditioning wider use on public consent. Establishes Kent as a limited, consent-conditioned user with no London-facing deployment.

sources.title: London cops bring live facial recognition to West End (The Register)
sources.what_it_supports: Establishes that fixed/static LFR inside London is a Metropolitan Police programme - lamppost-mounted cameras in the West End and Soho by the end of 2026, following the Croydon static pilot - and contains no mention of the City of London or City of London Police, supporting the finding that the Square Mile is outside the static rollout.

sources.title: Summary of judgment: Thompson and Carlo v Metropolitan Police Commissioner (Judiciary of England and Wales)
sources.what_it_supports: The 21 April 2026 High Court decision upholding the Met's LFR policy against Article 8/10/11 challenge - the permissive legal backdrop for every force in this item.

sources.title: Facial recognition technology in policing (POST, UK Parliament)
sources.what_it_supports: The national legal and governance picture: the distinction between live, retrospective and operator-initiated facial recognition, the absence of dedicated statute, the Home Office consultation opened at the end of 2025 and the legislation announced in the May 2026 King's Speech but not yet laid.
